linkedin.text:
In 2005, merchants sued Visa and Mastercard over card fees.
On Monday, 21 years later, a federal judge in Brooklyn holds the final hearing on a proposed settlement.

Judge Brian Cogan gave the deal preliminary approval in June, calling it "fair, reasonable, and adequate." If he approves it for good, credit card swipe fees drop 0.1 percentage point for 5 years, and standard consumer cards get a 1.25% rate for 8 years. Shops could also turn down some premium and commercial credit cards, and add a surcharge or offer a discount on credit cards.

In plain money, 0.1 point is $10 on every $10,000 of credit card sales. A shop with $500,000 a year in credit card sales would pay about $500 a year less, if the full cut reaches its rate.

About 1,000 merchants, Walmart among them, asked the judge to say no. Merchant groups say the cut would only take the average rate back to its 2023 level. Visa and Mastercard are urging him to approve it.

I'd take the $500. I started SVPay because a cut of every sale shouldn't be the only way a shop gets paid. When customers pay with SVPay instead of a card, the shop pays 0% in processing fees and $0 to cash out; SVPay makes money from paid software plans instead.

Whatever happens Monday, ask your processor this week if your rate will drop by the full 0.1 point. And if the deal lets you turn down premium rewards cards, will you?

#SmallBusiness #Payments

facts.text: The interchange-fee litigation against Visa and Mastercard dates to 2005 (Payments Dive: 'litigation dating to mid-2005'; 'The litigation dates to 2005')

Visa-Mastercard Rule 23(b)(2) settlement, In re Payment Card Interchange Fee and Merchant Discount Antitrust Litigation, MDL 1720 (E.D.N.Y.): preliminary approval June 9, 2026 by U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan; final approval hearing set for Monday, Nov 16, 2026 in Brooklyn; not yet final. Re-checked Nov 12, 2026: the Nov 11 report still lists the Nov 16 hearing. The official settlement site (www.interchangeequitablereliefsettlement.com) could not be fetched from this run (client error), and PACER is not reachable, so the status rests on the two reports.
Judge Brian Cogan granted preliminary approval in June 2026 and called the settlement 'fair, reasonable, and adequate'
The settlement would trim credit interchange (swipe) fee rates by 10 basis points, 0.1 percentage point, for five years
It would impose a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards for eight years
It would give merchants the right to decline some higher-cost Visa and Mastercard premium and commercial credit cards
Merchants would gain new rights to add surcharges and offer discounts for credit cards
Walmart and about 1,000 other merchants asked the judge to reject final approval (978 signers on the Sept 10 objection letter, plus Walmart)
Merchant objectors say the rate cut 'would merely return the average Visa/Mastercard rate to its 2023 level' (paraphrased in the posts, no quotation marks)
facts.quote: would merely return the average Visa/Mastercard rate to its 2023 level

facts.text: Visa and Mastercard urged the court to grant final approval (filing a month before the Nov 16 hearing)
Worked example: $500,000 a year in credit card sales x 0.1 percentage point = $500 a year, if the full cut reaches the shop's rate
Example rates for the worked example: a 2.5% rate falling 0.1 percentage point to 2.4%

SVPay pricing (approved line, checks/approved_lines.json pricing_one_line): 0% processing fees and $0 to cash out on payments made with SVPay, on every plan; SVPay makes money from paid software plans
